title: Dual-mode dynamics in hippocampal populations enable rapid and precise spatial coding
abstract: Hippocampal spatial representations emerge within minutes of first exposure to novel environments, challenging models based solely on gradual synaptic plasticity. Here, we show that CA1 spatial coding is organized according to a dual-mode architecture comprising a pre-organized backbone and an experience-dependent component. Backbone cells expressing immediately emerging place fields form a stable spatial scaffold and dominate positional decoding from the first traversal, whereas experience-dependent cells bearing gradually emerging fields are progressively incorporated to refine spatial representations. Analyses of ensemble activity further reveal that offline dynamics prospectively organize future spatial coding. In backbone cells, latent tuning aligns with their future place fields prior to task engagement, while in experience-dependent cells this alignment strengthens before overt place-field expression. Together, these findings identify a dual-mode organization of hippocampal populations in which offline dynamics pre-organize network activity to enable rapid and precise spatial coding in novel environments.

title: The chytrid fungus threatens the last epidemiologically naive Neotropical montane amphibian biodiversity hotspot
abstract: The amphibian chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (B. dendrobatidis) has caused catastrophic biodiversity loss worldwide. 1 , 2 , 3 Although B. dendrobatidis is now widespread across environmentally suitable regions, 4 the absence of amphibian declines in some high-suitability areas suggests the existence of refuges supporting epidemiologically naive communities. Epidemiologically naive refuges have not experienced past B. dendrobatidis epizootics despite suitable environmental conditions and may be B. dendrobatidis-free, harbor less virulent B. dendrobatidis lineages, or contain resistant host communities. As eradication of virulent B. dendrobatidis lineages is rarely successful after establishment, identifying epidemiologically naive refuges is imperative. 5 , 6 Here, following extensive multi-year disease surveillance, we report a major epidemiologically naive refuge in the Neotropical highlands, the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (SNSM) in northern Colombia. We found no evidence for contemporary B. dendrobatidis presence, despite detecting the hypervirulent Global Panzootic Lineage in a neighboring Andean mountain range. Population genomic analyses in SNSM-endemic harlequin toads found no demographic signatures indicative of cryptic epizootic decline. Niche modeling predicted high suitability for B. dendrobatidis occurrence and B. dendrobatidis-induced declines throughout the SNSM, with climatic conditions in lowland regions surrounding the SNSM likely acting as a dispersal barrier and preventing B. dendrobatidis invasion, creating a "sky island." Infection trials using three SNSM-endemic amphibian species revealed tolerant and susceptible species. Together, our results indicate that the SNSM is an epidemiologically naive refuge at risk of invasion by hypervirulent B. dendrobatidis, which could result in the loss of 25 endemic amphibian species. We highlight the urgent need for proactive conservation action and the strict implementation of biosecurity to safeguard the unique and vast amphibian diversity of the SNSM.

title: A North American mycorrhizal fungus displays zinc tolerance intraspecific variation and protects pines from zinc toxicity
abstract: Soil zinc (Zn) pollution, largely caused by anthropogenic activities such as mining and metal processing, can disrupt metabolism and reproduction, often leading to death. Some fungi can tolerate elevated Zn concentrations, but the mechanisms of Zn tolerance and if and how they affect symbionts are still unclear. To fill these gaps in knowledge, we investigated Zn tolerance in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Suillus tomentosus and its host pine Pinus contorta, two widespread symbiotic partners in American Western forests. Using a combination of whole-genome resequencing, in vitro Zn fungal assays, fungal-pine partner bioassays, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, we found an absence of S. tomentosus population structure based on Zn tolerance, and that the trait is highly polygenic, constitutive, and associated with Zn exclusion and antioxidant responses to mitigate toxicity. We also found that S. tomentosus protects P. contorta from Zn toxicity by increasing seedling performance under Zn stress, with Zn-tolerant S. tomentosus providing slightly more benefit compared with Zn-sensitive S. tomentosus. Our results illustrate that fungal metal tolerance is a complex trait, and that intraspecific variation should be considered for understanding the impacts of environmental stress on biodiversity, as well as for designing effective biotechnological tools and conservation/reforestation strategies.

title: A premitotic polarity program patterns the grass leaf epidermis
abstract: Transverse asymmetric cell divisions (ACDs) in grass leaf epidermal development produce large basal pavement cells and small apical specialized cells. These "patterning divisions" generate the long-short epidermal cell pattern that is distinctive of grasses. Here, we show that patterning divisions require premitotic basal polarization of BdPOLAR-LIKE1 (BdPL1) in the model grass Brachypodium distachyon. Loss of BdPL1 disrupted division-plane orientation and postmitotic cell-size asymmetry in all cell files, which resulted in epidermal patterning defects. Ectopic expression analyses demonstrated that BdPL1 polarization was independent of cellular context and sufficient to promote supernumerary transverse divisions. Furthermore, the developmental regulators BdBREVIS RADIX-solo and BdYODA1 formed a post-division polarity domain that enforced cell fate asymmetry independently of BdPL1. We propose that the premitotic BdPL1 module enforces physical cell division asymmetry contributing to medio-lateral patterning of cell types, whereas the postmitotic BdBRX-solo/BdYDA1 module enforces within-file cell fate asymmetry. Together, they robustly pattern the grass leaf epidermis.

title: Mucoromycotina fine root endophyte engages in a nutritionally mutualistic symbiosis with Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: Arabidopsis thaliana, a widely used genetic model species, is considered incapable of forming mycorrhizal associations, which support nutrient acquisition in most other land plants. Mucoromycotina "fine root endophytes" (MFREs) are a recently characterized group of mycorrhizal fungi capable of forming nutritional mutualisms with a wide range of plants, supplying nitrogen and phosphorus to host plants and gaining access to photosynthetically derived carbon. Here, we demonstrate that a wild-isolated MFRE strain, Lyc-1, successfully colonizes Arabidopsis roots under monoaxenic conditions without affecting plant growth. Using a combination of conventional light and epifluorescence microscopy, we demonstrate extensive extra- and intraradical colonization of the root cortex. Stable- and radio-isotope tracing further revealed bidirectional nutrient exchange between the host plant and the fungus. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a functional, mycorrhiza-like nutritional mutualism in Arabidopsis. As Arabidopsis lacks a complete set of common symbiosis signaling pathway genes, our findings suggest that Arabidopsis-Lyc-1 symbiosis may be controlled by an alternative, so far uncharacterized, symbiotic pathway. Thus, our study not only supports the existence of multiple evolutionary routes to plant-fungal nutritional mutualisms but also establishes Arabidopsis as a genetically tractable model to study plant-fungal symbiosis, thereby opening new opportunities to dissect the molecular basis and evolution of mycorrhizal symbioses.

title: Neural coordination of wing and leg movements during a terrestrial threat display
abstract: In most flying species, legs and wings mediate earthbound vs. aerial locomotion, respectively. During terrestrial social displays such as threat or courtship, however, species-typical movements of these appendages are coordinated in a stereotyped manner. How such appendicular control is integrated is poorly understood. Threat behavior in Drosophila consists of four types of leg and wing actions, which can be performed singly or in combination. Using a large-scale functional screen, we previously identified a cluster of 4-5 AIP (CL062) neurons whose optogenetic activation can evoke all threat actions and which are essential for natural threat displays. To understand how this threat command module functions, we have mapped AIP neurons into the male fly connectome and identified split-GAL4 drivers for four major downstream targets, whose functional connectivity and behavioral roles we have tested. Surprisingly, we find that distinct threat-specific actions are not controlled by parallel connections from different subsets of AIP cells to different action-specific descending neurons (DNs), a parsimonious circuit architecture. Rather, AIP neurons collectively activate two parallel downstream modules comprising pairs of neurons that control wing vs. leg movements, respectively. Wing movements are controlled via direct projections to two specialist DNs that act synergistically, while leg movements are controlled indirectly via two interneurons that act antagonistically to pattern the activity of multiple DNs, which are likely used in other locomotor contexts. These data elucidate a hierarchical circuit for appendicular coordination during a terrestrial social display and provide insight into how the brain has repurposed appendage-specific locomotor control for social communication, a form of exaptation.

title: Longitudinal study of Toba/Qom communities reveals delay and shortening of sleep in real time
abstract: While artificial light and digital technologies are widely assumed to delay and curtail sleep, direct, longitudinal evidence documenting these changes is remarkably scarce. From 2012 to 2024, we conducted a longitudinal study of native Toba/Qom communities in northern Argentina, including rural groups newly introduced to electricity and semi-urban groups with earlier access to electricity. Using linear mixed-effects models on a dataset of over 12,000 actigraphically recorded sleep events from 156 participants at different times, we observed striking shifts in sleep dynamics. Remarkably, both groups showed delays of close to 1 h in sleep timing, and participants from rural communities lost 35 min of sleep within the course of a decade. These changes occurred across a period that included, first, the introduction of electricity to rural communities after 2016, and, in more recent years, the spread of the internet and smartphone use among the Toba/Qom. While previous work in these and other populations has shown that both factors are associated with changes in sleep habits, our analyses suggest that they cannot fully explain the reported shifts in sleep timing across time by themselves, which may therefore be consistent with concurrent broader processes of modernization and acculturation. These transformations highlight the rapid changes that can take place in communities going through the early stages of the adoption of modern technologies, offering a contemporary parallel to the shifts in human sleep hypothesized to have accompanied global industrialization.

title: An ancient polymorphism in myosin I a/b determines chiral variation in Japanese Euhadra snails
abstract: Left-right (LR) asymmetry is a fundamental feature of animal development, yet progress in understanding its establishment has been limited by the fact that almost all animals do not ordinarily vary in the direction of their asymmetry. Snails are an exception because some wild-living species show abundant variation-externally visible in the shell coiling direction or "chirality"-yet the existing knowledge is from species, including the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, in which the sinistral mutation is rare and causes pathology. Here, we show that chiral polymorphism in Japanese Euhadra snails is due to functional variation in an unconventional myosin I a/b, a myosin family member not previously implicated in LR specification in any animal. Both the sinistral and dextral gene variants are ancient, impart minimal transcriptional differences in the single-cell embryo, and are not associated with pathology. Analyses show that relaxed selection enabled dominant-acting amino acid substitutions in the sinistral version of the Euhadra myosin motor domain and motor-lever junction, potentially affecting actomyosin interactions. For comparison, in the pond snail, we found that thousands of genes are differentially expressed between dextral and sinistral embryos due to the frameshift mutation in a formin gene. Overall, these results reinforce the role of myosin and actin-driven processes in LR symmetry breaking, broaden the known molecular repertoire, and highlight key mutations and positions in myosins that should be explored further, including in other animals. VIDEO ABSTRACT.

title: Hunger recruits a parallel circuit encoding alcohol reward
abstract: Internal states like hunger, pain, thirst, and arousal can bias behavior by affecting sensory and memory processing. Internal states are critical to understand in the context of alcohol addiction because they influence cravings, reinstatement, and relapse. Norepinephrine plays a key role in both hunger and alcohol-induced arousal and preference, but the circuit-level mechanisms through which it modulates the influence of hunger on alcohol preference are not well understood. We sought to address this using intersectional genetic tools for manipulating neurons expressing octopamine, the invertebrate analog of vertebrate norepinephrine. We identified a single octopamine neuron required for ethanol seeking only when Drosophila are food deprived. Hunger increased baseline activity in this neuron, thus making it more responsive to an odor cue previously paired with ethanol. A combination of genetic and connectome analyses revealed that the synaptic partners of this octopaminergic neuron form a functional module that acts on Drosophila memory circuitry. Thus, we show that hunger recruits a parallel circuit that drives learned ethanol preference, providing a neuronal framework through which internal state influences the expression of memory for ethanol-associated cues. VIDEO ABSTRACT.

title: Electrical synapses mediate visual orientation behavior
abstract: Animals constantly detect and orient toward salient visual objects, but the neural circuits underlying this process remain poorly understood. We previously showed that T3 neurons, a visual columnar cell type in Drosophila melanogaster , drive saccadic orientation toward visual landmarks during flight. Here, we identify LC17 neurons, a visual projection cell type, as T3 downstream partners for saccadic visual orientation. Using in vivo optical physiology and virtual reality behavior, we demonstrate that LC17 neurons are broadly tuned to visual objects and necessary for object tracking during flight. Notably, this tracking behavior depends on electrical synapses. We show that the innexin Shaking B (ShakB), which forms gap junctions in the fly brain, is highly expressed in LC17 dendrites. Additionally, LC17-specific knockdown of shakB perturbs the cell physiological visual response and impairs the behavioral readout of object motion vision for saccadic orientation. Our findings reveal the mechanisms underlying visual orientation and highlight the interplay between electrical and chemical neurotransmission for object detection and rapid action selection.

title: Functional roles of abyssal benthos in sustaining polymetallic nodule fields
abstract: Polymetallic nodules form a critical habitat in the abyssal plain ecosystems where they occur, supporting high benthic biodiversity. They form over millions of years in areas of extremely low sedimentation rates, but it is unclear how the nodules remain on the surface, and hence available for benthic biota. Here, we use seabed time-lapse photography to explore the potential role of benthic fauna in the maintenance of polymetallic nodules on the seabed surface. We observed several species directly removing sediment from the nodule surface, mainly holothurians and gastropods, and infauna bioturbation causing nodule uplifting. Derived estimates of the area covered by animal movements, as a proxy for bioturbation, indicated that a maximum of one to two decades is needed to clear sediment from and uplift all nodules of the field of the view. This study provides the first empirical evidence that bioturbation by these animals, significantly influences hard substratum dynamics. If these behaviours significantly counteract nodule burial over the long term, bioturbation may be a key mechanism in nodule maintenance, as hypothesized for over 40 years. This essential (and measurable) function for the maintenance of abyssal biodiversity in nodule-field seascapes has been largely overlooked, highlighting that substantial gaps of knowledge subsist in our understanding of the functioning of nodule field ecosystems. Improving assessment of habitat engineers may enhance predictions of ecosystem resilience if commercial mining activities occur. However, this study opens new opportunities for benthic monitoring framed towards the acquisition of a more holistic understanding of abyssal ecosystem dynamics and functioning.

title: Bioturbation
abstract: Bioturbation is an umbrella term for the biological reworking of soils and sediments by all kinds of organisms. It includes not only the impact of animals, but also that of rooting plants and trees. Although Charles Darwin's last scientific book On the Formation of Vegetable Mounds through the Action of Worms with Observations on their Habits (1881) already reported pioneering observations on the role of earthworms in particle displacement, soil formation and erosion-sedimentation processes, the term bioturbation was only introduced 70 years later to describe fossil biogenic structures in sedimentary rocks. We now know that bioturbation plays a major role in soil formation, geomorphology, sediment stability, structure and texture, and impacts the distribution, diversity and functioning of microbes and global biogeochemical cycles. As such, bioturbation is studied by biologists, ecologists, soil scientists, sedimentologists, biogeochemists, civil and environmental engineers, paleontologists and paleoceanographers. Here we focus on bioturbation by animals in the Earth's largest ecosystem, the seafloor, but bioturbation is also a key factor in freshwater sediments, wetlands and terrestrial soils.

title: Anthropogenic novel entities in the Earth system
abstract: The term 'novel entities' refers to anthropogenic substances and materials that have the potential to disrupt natural processes across the spheres of Earth - the lithosphere (land), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), and biosphere (living things). The 'planetary boundaries framework', within which novel entities were defined, identifies boundaries of the safe operating space of Earth, which, if crossed, may lead to dangerous and irreversible changes. Generally, novel entities of planetary concern are those substances that are persistent, mobile, and potentially harmful. Novel entities include new chemicals, modified life forms, and engineered materials (Figure 1).

title: The deep-time history of soils and plants
abstract: For a large community of ecosystem ecologists, plant-soil interactions have moved center stage in the understanding of both plant and soil ecology. Frequently, plants are deemed to be the main drivers of these interactions. However, soils existed before the evolution of land plants (i.e., embryophytes), and terrestrial communities were already highly diverse around 400 million years ago (Ma), reflecting an earlier origin of the organisms that populated them. But which organisms were contemporaneous at the origin of soil and in what type of environment they lived is not well established. Here, we trace the development of soil and its biotic components from the beginnings, about one billion years ago (Ga), by using the fossil record and geochemical data. We show that the first terrestrial ecosystems were probably situated near the ocean, where organisms were already adapted to high oxygen pressures and where plants were not yet present. Drawing on this, we discuss the need to rethink the primacy of plants in modern terrestrial ecosystems, considering that persistence of the soil system over deep time could help explain the enormous current biodiversity found in soil. We advocate for a shift in perspective by embracing a vision of terrestrial ecosystems with interdependent and equally important above- and below-ground system compartments. Finally, we highlight the importance of 'bending the curve' on the increasing rate of soil degradation and loss of soil health, and we discuss the outlook for the future of soils and their interactions with plants.

title: Deep microbial biosphere
abstract: The deep microbial biosphere is a vast ecosystem extending kilometers beneath Earth's surface in terrestrial rocks, aquifers, marine sediments, and oceanic crust. Blocked from sunlight, and often severely limited in organic carbon and oxygen, these environments host microorganisms sustained by energy sources such as hydrogen gas, reduced metals, and sulfur compounds. Over the past few decades, advances in sampling, cultivation-independent methods, and deep-sea drilling have revealed diverse bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic life in the subsurface, including still poorly understood lineages with unusual metabolic strategies. Despite extreme energy limitation and often harsh conditions, subsurface microorganisms persist through adaptations and strategies such as metabolic versatility, streamlined genomes, efficient carbon fixation pathways, and slow growth. Collectively, microbial communities exert an important yet poorly constrained influence on Earth's long-term carbon, sulfur, and nitrogen cycles. Although uncertainties remain related to rates of metabolic activity, generation times, and global contributions to biogeochemical cycles, the deep biosphere has emerged as a central component of Earth's biosphere and is growing in relevance as human activities increasingly intersect with the deep subsurface.

title: Birds shape biogeochemistry and ecosystem function globally
abstract: Birds inhabit nearly every environment on Earth, shaping ecosystems through diverse functions that include contributions to biogeochemical cycles. By transporting and recycling nutrients, birds influence the availability and distribution of chemical elements that regulate key ecological processes. Yet, as bird populations decline, their biogeochemical roles remain poorly synthesized, limiting our understanding of the broader consequences of biodiversity loss. Here, we systematically review the role of birds in biogeochemistry, with consequences for ecosystem function, structure, and connectivity globally. We highlight key mechanisms, ecological impacts, and future research and management priorities. We find that birds - by virtue of their broad distribution and abundance, flight-enabled mobility, nutrient-rich diets, and high metabolic demands - play distinct roles in nutrient transport. Although research has focused largely on waterbirds, growing evidence reveals birds' substantial chemical impacts on diverse environments, locally restructuring plant, microbial, and animal communities. Delivery of key limiting elements, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, can boost primary productivity and increase autotroph nutrient content, with bottom-up effects on higher trophic levels. However, bird subsidies can also promote soil acidification, contaminant accumulation, plant damage, and eutrophication. Because birds vary in their diet, size, life history, and behavior, declines in diversity can trigger uneven and cascading ecosystem effects. Human-driven changes in bird abundance, distribution, movement, and nutrition are modifying and diminishing avian-mediated biogeochemical processes across the biosphere, with potential consequences for ecosystem fertility, productivity, functional connectivity, and carbon storage. Nevertheless, opportunities remain to harness bird biogeochemistry in ecological restoration to revitalize Earth's natural nutrient networks.

title: Navigation map has to be learned by migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers
abstract: It used to be thought that young migrating birds perform their first migration using an innate 'clock-and-compass' programme that specifies the timing of onset of movement and its direction and duration, but did not require information about the bird's current position 1 . In classic displacement experiments, young birds continued to fly in their normal migratory direction, whereas adults were able to adjust their course after displacement 2 . More recent evidence, however, suggests that young birds may estimate their position and adjust their behaviour when delayed or displaced, even during their maiden flight 3 , 4 . Evidence for innate magnetic map responses in hatchling sea turtles and juvenile salmonids 5 suggests that birds may also inherit magnetic positional information. We have investigated this hypothesis in the Eurasian reed warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus), a species in which compensation for physical and virtual magnetic displacement has been demonstrated in experienced migrants 6 , 7 . We used migration-naïve birds trapped in early autumn as juveniles and kept in captivity over winter. In spring, the birds were tested first in the natural magnetic field at Rybachy in Russia, and then under a virtual magnetic displacement to Keele, UK. Under the virtual magnetic displacement, the birds did not change their orientation as expected if they possessed a magnetic map. We found no evidence that migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers use a functional innate magnetic map under the conditions of our experiment. In this species, the first migration is guided primarily by an inherited compass programme, whereas a functional magnetic map develops through migratory experience.

title: Neuroimmune signaling: Dopamine release from fat tissue mediates pathogen avoidance
abstract: Animals must quickly learn to avoid food that makes them sick. A recent study in Drosophila melanogaster shows that ingesting pathogenic bacteria triggers dopamine release from fat cells that alters odor responses in the fly brain and switches feeding preference toward non-pathogenic food.

title: Ecosystem engineering, regime shifts and the rise of animals
abstract: The term 'ecosystem engineering' refers to biotic processes that modulate the availability of resources to other species. These processes thus modify, maintain or create habitats and impact the abundance and diversity of species within ecosystems. In turn, the study of ecosystem engineering in the fossil record is leading to a re-evaluation of the influence of organisms on the deep-time evolution of Earth-system structure and function. With this comes a growing recognition that biological forces may be key drivers of major transitions in Earth history. There are two crucial questions: first, have new ecosystem engineering processes emerged randomly throughout geologic time, or are they clustered? Second, to what extent has their emergence driven episodes of evolutionary radiation or extinction? Here, we address these questions through the lens of the Ediacaran-Cambrian transition (∼575-530 million years ago) - an interval that witnessed the rapid rise of animals, following nearly four billion years of microbial dominance. We propose that an engineering regime shift occurred in the late Ediacaran that gave rise to new rules of community assembly, new ecological niches, and altered macroevolutionary trajectories. We argue that the recognition of ecosystem engineering regime shifts may help us not only to understand other key intervals in the Phanerozoic, but also to project the future of ecosystems under human influence.

title: Locomotor kinematics and head stabilization in rolling snakes
abstract: Morphology constrains the strategies available to organisms and their functional capacities. A striking example is the absence of wheels and the rarity of rolling locomotion across the animal kingdom 1 , 2 . Although rolling can confer high speed, it poses a fundamental mechanical challenge, as body rotation destabilizes the head and disrupts sensory-guided adjustment, particularly at high speeds. Here we report a behavioral solution to this problem: our video analyses show that dwarf reed snakes (Pseudorabdion) stabilize their head during dynamic rotational motion of the posterior body by using precisely coordinated body movements. This acrobatic behavior enables fast and controlled rolling locomotion that would otherwise be impossible, illustrating how behavioral innovation can circumvent deep morphological constraints and expand the capacities of animals.

title: Plant evolution: How duckweeds became so small
abstract: Duckweeds are highly reduced flowering plants with a simplified body plan. A new study reveals that the duckweed frond retains ancestral organ identities despite compression and fusion. Together with previous evidence of root loss, these findings highlight distinct evolutionary routes to plant miniaturization.

title: Crop engineering: Plant genes tied to the weather
abstract: Coupling of a late blight disease resistance gene to a humidity-responsive cis-element in potato achieves resistance under high-humidity conditions that favor disease. This strategy sidesteps the yield penalties associated with constitutive resistance gene expression.

title: Tectonics, geomorphology and biodiversity
abstract: The global distribution of biodiversity broadly follows latitude and climate with regions of high species richness in the tropics and environments rich in energy, water and other factors conducive to life. However, superimposed on the correlation with climate is a correspondence between biodiversity and physical geography. High biodiversity is also associated with mountain systems. The inference is that topographic relief generates ecological heterogeneity through the creation of complex topography, landforms and the interaction of that topography with climate, creating temperature and rainfall gradients, geographic barriers and habitat patchiness. All of these factors create new niches for species, driving formation of new species and thus biodiversity. Mountain ranges are the product of tectonic activity where mantle convection and tectonic plate motion have deformed the surface of the Earth, uplifting crustal rock and creating rugged topography and high relief. Tectonics creates topography, but surface processes, such as mineral weathering, physical erosion by wind, water and ice, as well as sediment transport and deposition, modify that topography. The result is the complex patchwork of landscapes of the Earth's surface whose description is at the core of the field of geomorphology. There is a vast complexity to the processes within tectonics, geomorphology, ecology and evolutionary biology, and the links between the physical and biological processes are only beginning to be understood. To complicate matters, these processes are time dependent, coupled and include multiple feedbacks. Mountain ranges rise and fall. Ocean basins open and close. Moving plates and active faults displace terrains or entire continents across climatic gradients or relative to each other. Rivers and valleys may connect regions, but rivers can be redirected, providing new connections bringing species into a common competitive arena, or closing connections, leaving populations isolated and free to evolve without competitive constraints. Biodiversity emerges from this continual interplay of tectonics, geomorphology, and ecology, with Earth's surface persistently creating and erasing opportunities for life to diversify.

title: Large animal restoration and carbon storage across climate-relevant timescales
abstract: By virtue of their size and mobility, large animals can play important roles in Earth's carbon cycle. This has led to suggestions that restoring their populations can contribute to mitigating the climate crisis through removal and storage of atmospheric carbon. However, as animals can affect both release and sequestration of carbon, understanding when, where and how much they impact climate-relevant carbon is critical for evaluating their potential to become a trustworthy climate nature-based solution. Here, we review scientific evidence for the carbon impacts of elephants and great whales - two well-studied animal groups commonly cited for climate mitigation and suggested for carbon monetization. We identify six lessons to guide future research, policy and practice: first, large animal carbon impacts vary considerably by individual, species, ecosystem and biospheric conditions, making predictions of future impacts hard and wildlife-based carbon investments high-risk; second, meaningful carbon impacts will likely take longer to manifest than the Paris Agreement's mid-century net-zero target, but wildlife restoration should nonetheless begin now to realize immediate co-benefits and potentially support longer-term climate recovery; third, current conservation remains highest priority, as loss of animals may exacerbate climate breakdown; fourth, caution is needed when incorporating wildlife into climate policy to prevent false confidence in mitigation potential or perverse outcomes; fifth, potential wildlife carbon benefits should be communicated transparently and cautiously to manage expectations; sixth, robust monitoring and validation are essential to ensure carbon sequestration is real and durable. With these lessons in mind, conservation and restoration of large animals may realize their potential to aid long-term climate recovery as well as ecological resilience and adaptation under ongoing global change.

title: The evolution of oxygen, temperature, and marine aerobic habitat for animals over the last billion years of Earth history
abstract: Atmospheric and ocean oxygen levels and temperature have changed considerably over Earth history, and many of these changes coincided with similarly dramatic changes in marine life. The synergistic interaction between oxygen availability and temperature sets aerobic capacities for marine animals, determining whether a given environment is habitable. Here, we explore the relationship between oxygen, temperature and aerobic habitability across the last billion years of Earth history using a metric known as the 'metabolic index' (Φ). Idealized scenarios for oxygen-temperature trajectories indicate several distinct avenues for a concurrent transition from 'non-permissive' to 'permissive' aerobic environments at the onset of the Cambrian Period. Thereafter, the continued presence of fossils in shallow, tropical habitats sets clear constraints on oxygen-temperature combinations, suggesting that the most extreme published estimates for each are improbable. We then draw on published oxygen and temperature estimates to illustrate how these variables have controlled aerobic habitability for marine animals over the Phanerozoic. The dominance of hypoxia-tolerant faunas during the Paleozoic is explained in part by low oxygen oceans, while increasing oxygen levels in the Devonian likely led to lower extinction rates. Sharp spikes in temperature, such as during the end-Permian, led to the contraction of aerobic habitat and mass extinction, but probably also to a more temperature-tolerant modern fauna. We emphasize the need for more robust environmental records of early animal evolution and a better understanding of trade-offs in animal physiology. Finally, exciting future applications of the metabolic index to astrobiology have arisen as knowledge of extraterrestrial environmental conditions increases.

title: Astrobiology
abstract: Astrobiology aims not only to determine whether life exists beyond Earth but to understand how biology 'fits' into a physicochemical universe of stars and planets, including Earth itself. The field coalesced in the late twentieth century around a core of much older questions about the origin, evolution, distribution and future of life in the universe. Today, it is a rapidly advancing interdisciplinary collaboration that draws on many sources of data - from planetary missions and exoplanet surveys to field-based, experimental, computational and analytical methods in biology, geology, chemistry, physics and astronomy. A recurrent concern across many branches of astrobiology is the fuzziness of the boundaries between life and non-life as well as the difficulty of discriminating biological signals from an 'abiotic baseline'.

title: Depression: Ketamine quiets an unruly habenula
abstract: Ketamine's robust antidepressant effects often appear twenty-four hours after a single dose. A new study now provides evidence suggesting that this timepoint coincides with a quieting of habenula activation and reductions in aversive learning in healthy subjects.

title: Chunking: What working memory gains and loses
abstract: Chunking compresses information into fewer meaningful units, reducing working memory demands. During chunking, neural representations in the prefrontal cortex exhibit reduced dimensionality and are biased toward chunk centers, suggesting lossy compression that improves overall retention while reducing precision within chunks.

title: Trace fossils
abstract: Ichnology (from the ancient Greek ichnos, a footprint or track) is the study of ichnofossils, or trace fossils. These are all the fossils that cannot be called 'body fossils' (skeletons, shells, preserved bodies and body parts). Trace fossils are typically tracks, trails or burrows, and they provide information on ancient environments and ancient behaviour. Ichnologists and palaeobiologists can identify whether a suite of trace fossils was produced in an ancient desert or on the deep abyssal ocean floor. Even more startling is that a trackway of dinosaur footprints can reveal the animal's speed, or even a behavioural shift like walking to the edge of a lake and then leaping in and swimming away.

title: Jiayang Li
abstract: Jiayang Li received his master's degree from the Institute of Genetics (now the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, IGDB), Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) in 1984 and his PhD from Brandeis University in 1991. He subsequently undertook postdoctoral research on plant molecular genetics at the Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant Research at Cornell University. He has been a Professor at IGDB since 1994, served as Vice President of CAS (2003-2011) and President of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (2011-2016), and has been Director General of the Yazhouwan National Laboratory since 2022. His research focuses on the molecular basis of complex traits regulating high yield, superior quality, and strong resilience, and breeding elite rice varieties by rational design. He has been elected as a member or associate member of CAS (2001), the World Academy of Sciences (TWAS; 2004), the US National Academy of Sciences (NAS; 2011), the German Academy of Sciences (2012), and the UK Royal Society (2015).

title: What the trees remember
Gaia with a thousand faces
abstract: Life and Earth are intimately connected — a connection we have long overlooked at our peril. It is the core of the ‘ Gaia hypothesis' — the notion that Life and Earth act as a unit to self-regulate planetary conditions so they remain favorable for life's persistence. A shape-shifting, amorphous entity, straddling scientific disciplines and audiences, the Gaia hypothesis has a complex history: disdained in some scientific disciplines, foundational in others and enthusiastically endorsed further afield. Lately, renewed scientific interest and a more consilient view of Gaia is emerging, precipitated not least by the planetary polycrisis. Florian Maderspacher on Gaia 's many guises.

title: A planet shaped by life
Interbacterial competition triggers stress-induced CRISPR immunity against bacteriophages
abstract: Bacteria-phage interactions are often studied in relatively simple experimental systems involving a single bacterial strain infected by a single phage. 1 1. Alseth, E.O. ∙ Pursey, E. ∙ Luján, A.M. ... Bacterial biodiversity drives the evolution of CRISPR-based phage resistance Nature. 2019; 574 :549-552 Crossref Scopus (114) PubMed Google Scholar However, it remains unknown whether competition also alters the initial generation of CRISPR immunity by changing CRISPR-Cas expression and spacer acquisition before selection among resistance phenotypes occurs. Here, we show that interbacterial competition can trigger CRISPR-Cas activation and adaptation in P. aeruginosa . When co-cultured with Acinetobacter baumannii , P. aeruginosa exhibited markedly increased expression of CRISPR-Cas genes and a higher frequency of new spacer acquisition, whereas no such induction occurred in monoculture or mixed communities lacking A. baumannii . This upregulation was associated with markers of DNA damage and stress signaling, indicating that competition-induced stress primes the bacterial adaptive immune response. These findings identify interbacterial antagonism as an ecological and physiological trigger for CRISPR activation, linking competitive interactions to enhanced antiphage defense. More broadly, our results suggest that bacteria sense and respond to competitive stress in complex microbial communities by increasing the generation of more adapted genotypes.

title: Dynamic roles of embryonic glial cells in octopus brain development
abstract: Coleoid cephalopods, such as octopus, squid, and cuttlefish, have evolved remarkably large nervous systems with neuron numbers comparable to those of small mammals. Despite this, little is known about how these nervous systems develop, which genetic programs drive the formation and diversification of their neural cells, and what factors contribute to evolutionary brain expansion. This study combined single-cell multi-omics with spatial expression analysis to uncover the cell types and the regulatory mechanisms underlying nervous system development and evolution in Octopus vulgaris. We discovered an early embryonic glial cell population that is distinct from neurogenic progenitors and defined by orphan nuclear receptor 4a (nr4a), distal-less homeobox (dlx), and prospero homeobox (pros) regulons. Their spatial distribution and dynamic transcriptional profile during embryogenesis indicated that these cells might orchestrate cell migration, axon guidance, and brain patterning before expressing neuronal markers or differentiating into mature glia. Comparison of embryonic glial transcriptional signatures across two cephalopods, a gastropod, and Drosophila revealed shared expression of nr4a, dlx, and pros in mollusks, while embryonic glia in Drosophila expressed pros, dlx, repo, ttk, and gcm but not nr4a. Intriguingly, the overall gene expression profile of cephalopod embryonic glia has diverged from that of Pomacea canaliculata (golden apple snail), whose glia do not express guidance or patterning genes. Together, these findings identified a conserved embryonic glial cell type in mollusks that might have acquired new functions in coleoid cephalopods to organize neuronal migration and wiring in their expanded brain.

title: Integration of hydrogen peroxide sensing and detoxification by the C. elegans nervous system
abstract: Hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is the most common reactive chemical threat organisms face. Here, we map the neural circuit that drives chemotactic escape from environmental H 2 O 2 in the nematode C. elegans. Twenty-four neuron classes with sensory endings at the mouth and nose respond to H 2 O 2 , with dynamics encoding stimulus intensity and exposure history. Sensing begins when H 2 O 2 oxidizes the peroxidatic and resolving cysteines of the cytosolic peroxiredoxin PRDX-2, which relays this oxidative signal to cysteines on the LITE-1 and GUR-3 ion channels, triggering calcium influx in sensory neurons that drive escape. Most of these neurons release glutamate to drive H 2 O 2 -dependent excitation of AIA interneurons, whereas others signal through non-glutamatergic routes. Thus, the C. elegans nervous system monitors H 2 O 2 -induced changes in the intracellular H 2 O 2 -detoxification machinery and relays them to interneurons driving organism-wide escape. This raises the possibility that changes in neuronal activity in aging and neurodegenerative diseases arise from altered peroxiredoxin-mediated H 2 O 2 signaling rather than primarily from direct macromolecular damage by H 2 O 2 .

title: Selective control of course correction over long timescales in the Drosophila central complex
abstract: The insect central complex governs intricate navigational behaviors. One key region of the central complex, the fan-shaped body (FB), is where movement decisions are computed during goal-directed behaviors. However, our knowledge of when FB circuits are deployed is limited, and the FB has only been directly implicated in a few, narrowly defined behaviors. Here, we demonstrate that FB circuits affect course-correcting movements that, over long timescales, align the fly's heading with the perceived direction of optic flow. Silencing a major input neuronal population to the FB, the PFN d neurons, abolishes this behavior while leaving certain reflexive turning behaviors intact. Further, introduction of a fictive error signal in either the PFN d or PFN a neurons via optogenetic activation reveals that they are sufficient to affect the forward movement of the fly while slightly biasing its heading direction. We propose a model whereby the fly recruits the circuitry of the central complex to selectively influence features of movement that emerge over long timescales.

title: Top-down inferior colliculus signals engage unipolar brush cell circuits in the dorsal cochlear nucleus of the mouse auditory system
abstract: Sensory systems comprise ascending pathways that convey information from the sense organs and descending pathways that provide feedback and contextual signals to guide sensory processing. How top-down signals are integrated at early stages to improve sensory function remains poorly understood. The dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) is a cerebellum-like circuit proposed to perform adaptive filtering, including suppression of self-generated sounds. A major question is how sound-frequency-specific top-down information is processed by the DCN, since many top-down inputs target granule cells whose axons span the tonotopic axis and are unlikely to maintain frequency-specific signals. Here, we characterize neurons in the inferior colliculus that provide descending input to DCN. We show that among their targets are unipolar brush cells (UBCs) that distribute and transform descending signals directly to principal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in a circuit that bypasses granule cells. In vivo activation of UBCs attenuated auditory responses in awake mice. Together, these findings identify a circuit through which top-down signals from IC could influence early auditory processing and potentially guide adaptive filtering in the DCN.

title: Females shape hunting of vertebrates in wild bonobos
abstract: Hunting and meat consumption are widely considered key drivers of human evolution, and hypotheses about their origins draw on comparisons with our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos. These comparisons typically set up a behavioral dichotomy in which chimpanzees are characterized by cooperative hunting of arboreal primates by male-dominated parties, whereas bonobo hunts are thought to involve the opportunistic targeting of terrestrial ungulates, primarily by individual females. 1 , 2 , 3 Observations from two habituated bonobo communities at LuiKotale covering 10 years challenge this dichotomy. LuiKotale bonobos hunted both terrestrial ungulates (42%) and arboreal primates (43% of vertebrate prey), with red colobus monkeys comprising the majority of primate prey (77%). Males and females hunted arboreal primates at similar rates, and females accounted for most non-primate captures. Female age affected the hunting frequency of primates and ungulates, with the former being biased to younger and the latter to older females. The prominent role of female bonobos in hunting supports predictions that relate hunting activity to intersexual dominance relations rather than risk aversion, with the dominant sex being more active. Comparing data from neighboring communities revealed differences and suggests that social and environmental parameters affect prey choice by each community in different ways. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that chimpanzee-like, male-biased hunting represents the ancestral condition. They highlight the contribution of females to obtaining vertebrate prey, call for a reassessment of the role of females in hunting and meat sharing, and by extension, the framing of models of early hominin subsistence and social organization.

title: A language-model approach to species distribution reveals alternative stable states
abstract: Ecological communities are reorganizing rapidly under accelerating global change, yet predicting how species assemble, persist, or collapse remains a major challenge. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 Most species distribution models treat species as independent entities, overlooking the dependencies that structure ecological communities. Here, we introduce a language-model-inspired approach 5 , 6 to species distribution that generates ecological communities sequentially, predicting each species and its biomass conditional on previously assembled species. Trained on ∼27,000 reef fish surveys, 7 the generative framework reveals multiple coherent community configurations emerging under identical environmental conditions. 8 , 9 For instance, the model can generate both coral-associated and macroalgal-associated fish communities, consistent with alternative ecological regimes described in these ecosystems. The model also uncovers a hierarchy of emergent species positions within the learned dependency structure, including core species strongly associated with particular environmental conditions, bridging species linking alternative configurations, and satellite species occupying more peripheral positions. Despite this richer representation of ecological communities, the model also improves predictions of species occurrence and biomass relative to a species-by-species machine-learning baseline (XGBoost 10 ) and a multispecies deep-learning baseline (MLP 11 ). Together, these results show that ecological communities can be learned and generated as a structured syntax, from which multistability, directional assembly patterns, and hierarchical species positions naturally emerge.

title: Plant synergid embryonic potential is unlocked following egg cell collapse
abstract: Cell-cell communication is indispensable for cell specification and differentiation throughout plant reproduction. The egg cell and its sister synergid cell have long been considered closely coordinated partners during fertilization, yet the nature of this interplay and their specific roles remain unclear. Here, we show that synergid cells could acquire the competence to initiate cell division for embryogenesis following egg cell collapse. Unlike the traditional view, synergid cells appear to take over the egg cell role without undergoing fate conversion to adopt the egg cell identity. These findings suggest that synergid cells possess an intrinsic embryogenic potential, which is specifically unlocked upon egg cell collapse, thus enabling embryogenic initiation in the absence of a functional egg cell. Building on this discovery, we established an in planta haploid-induction system independent of conventional haploid-inducing genes. Importantly, this system also functions in tomato, a distantly related dicotyledonous crop, thus offering a broad conceptual framework for engineering haploid production across diverse plant species.

title: Dorsal forerunner cells couple epiboly movements to zebrafish notochord extension
abstract: Convergence and extension (C&E) cell movements promote anteroposterior axis extension and narrow both neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues during gastrulation. Mediolateral cell intercalation is largely responsible for this morphogenetic process in vertebrates, but evidence suggests that additional cell-extrinsic forces generated by surrounding tissues contribute to the shaping of many structures. In zebrafish, for example, mechanical forces generated by the anteriorly migrating prechordal plate cooperate with tissue-autonomous cell intercalations to promote extension of the notochord. Here, we propose a novel model for notochord morphogenesis by which epiboly forces within the enveloping layer are transmitted to the posterior end of the notochord via a cluster of dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) that physically links the two. We found that scattering or absence of DFCs caused by loss of crb2a or sox32, respectively, reduces notochord C&E and exacerbates axis extension defects in planar cell polarity signaling-deficient embryos. Using an automated image segmentation and cell shape analysis pipeline, we show that cells within the posterior notochord fail to properly elongate when DFCs are scattered or absent. Finally, we demonstrate that the loss of crb2a and sox32 fails to disrupt C&E of zebrafish embryonic explants in which no epiboly occurs and all extension is driven by cell-intrinsic behaviors. Together, these findings support a model in which DFCs facilitate mechanical coupling of the enveloping layer to the posterior notochord during epiboly to ensure its robust morphogenesis during gastrulation.

title: Alerting acoustic stimuli enhance the internal representation of head direction
abstract: Animals rapidly execute goal-directed spatial behaviors in response to threats, yet how alerting cues engage spatial representations remains unknown. Here, we tested whether head direction (HD) neurons-key components of the brain's navigation system-are recruited by alerting stimuli. We recorded thalamic and cortical HD cells in head-fixed mice during alerting acoustic stimuli while monitoring arousal via pupillometry and facial motion. Identified HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus exhibited ectopic axons and projections to the thalamic reticular nucleus. These cells responded to artificial and natural alerting sounds, with frequency tuning closely matching facial motion patterns. Thalamic responses comprised fast and slow components, whereas cortical responses in the dorsal presubiculum were sparser and dominated by the slow component. In the thalamus, the fast component was independent of HD tuning, whereas the slow component was selectively amplified by alerting stimuli. This gain modulation enhanced HD coding, with decoding accuracy scaling with facial motion. Together, these findings identify the thalamocortical HD system as a non-canonical auditory pathway relaying alerting signals to spatial navigation circuits, providing a mechanism by which alerting stimuli sharpen the internal compass for goal-directed behaviors.

title: A kleptomyiophilous orchid exploits milichiid flies through mimicry of common pentatomoid bugs with high levels of toxicity
abstract: To attract pollinators, mimetic flowers imitate the visual and olfactory cues that their pollinators use when responding to models. 1 , 2 However, it is unclear which processes influence the mimicry of particular models. One possibility is that selection favors mimicry of models that act as "magnet species" by attracting large numbers of potential pollinators. 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 According to this hypothesis, models should be highly common, even if they are not the most attractive resources. This may apply to kleptomyiophilous flowers that exploit kleptoparasitic flies by imitating injured insects. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 In this form of mimicry, the injured insect models would be highly common, even if they emit toxic defensive volatiles that could impede pollinator activities. 11 , 12 We report that the eastern ecotype of Bulbophyllum claviforme attracts a specific kleptoparasitic milichiid pollinator Phyllomyza sp. 1. Orchid floral scent is similar to (E)-2-decenal-dominated emissions of multiple pentatomoid bugs in the families Pentatomidae, Scutelleridae, Plataspidae, and Acanthosomatidae. Bioassays suggest that undecane, (E)-2-decenal and (E)-2-decenyl acetate are critical for attraction. Three (E)-2-alkenals, namely (E)-2-hexenal, (E)-2-octenal, and (E)-2-decenal, are both toxic and attractive to Phyllomyza sp. 1, with the toxicity of dominant (E)-2-alkenals negatively correlated to attractiveness. The orchid paradoxically appears to mimic pentatomoids that are less attractive due to higher toxicity. Selection may have favored mimicry of these bugs because (E)-2-decenal is emitted by a wide range of species, representing 68% of the pentatomoid species sampled. Our findings are congruent with the hypothesis that magnet species effects on pollinator abundance are important for the evolution of floral mimicry.

title: Allelic variation in OsATG3 enhances nitrogen-responsive tillering to sustain rice productivity
abstract: Nitrogen (N) deficiency constrains crop productivity by limiting shoot growth, yet the adaptive mechanisms that reprogram shoot development under low N conditions remain largely elusive. Here, we identify a major locus, OsATG3 (autophagy-related protein 3), controlling tillering in response to N deficiency through a genome-wide association study in rice. OsATG3 functions as an essential autophagy component and promotes selective degradation of IDEAL PLANT ARCHITECTURE1 (IPA1) via OsATG8d-mediated autophagy in shoot apices, thereby enhancing N-responsive tillering. Natural variation in the promoter of OsATG3 modulates its transcriptional activity and underlies the adaptive range of tiller number under low N conditions. The elite haplotype OsATG3-H enhances both tillering and grain yield under N-limited supply and appears to contribute to geographical adaptation both in O. sativa and O. glaberrima. Our findings uncover a genetic and molecular mechanism that couples N deficiency to shoot developmental plasticity, providing a promising target for sustainable rice breeding with reduced fertilizer input.

title: The antimicrobial peptide pileup promotes enterocyte shedding to maintain gut homeostasis in aging Drosophila
abstract: Cellular turnover is a fundamental biological process that counteracts aging by activating stem cells to replace aging cells. This process is especially critical for maintaining the intestinal epithelium, one of the most rapidly renewing tissues in the body. However, the replacement of aging enterocytes cannot be explained solely by the generation of new cells from intestinal stem cells (ISCs); it also requires the complementary process of physically removing aging enterocytes through shedding. Compared with the well-characterized regulation of ISCs, the mechanisms governing enterocyte shedding remain poorly understood. Here, we identify pileup, a novel age-associated antimicrobial peptide (AMP) in Drosophila, as both a genetic marker and a key regulator of enterocyte shedding. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated through age-related mitochondrial dysfunction, a process facilitated by Autophagy-related gene 1 (ATG1) kinase, activate hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, which induces pileup expression specifically in aging enterocytes. Pileup then compromises the membrane of these cells and triggers c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation, which we propose promotes their shedding. Notably, pileup has three homologs, and loss of all four genes leads to tumorous cell accumulation, gut barrier dysfunction, microbiome dysbiosis, and premature death. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for AMPs in the turnover of aging host cells, extending their classical function beyond microbial defense. This work provides new mechanistic insights into enterocyte shedding and underscores its essential role in preserving gut homeostasis during aging.

title: Avian germline-restricted chromosomes are reservoirs for active and expressed long-terminal-repeat retroviruses
abstract: Germline-restricted chromosomes (GRCs) occur only in germ cells and are absent from somatic cells in songbirds, but their contents and evolutionary mechanisms remain poorly understood. We performed comparative genomics on long-read GRC assemblies from male house finch (HF) (Haemorhous mexicanus), common rosefinch (RF) (Carpodacus erythrinus), and blue tit (Cyanistes caeruleus), the first two of which are newly assembled and annotated. The assemblies vary widely in size (6.5-168.4 Mb) and gene content; whereas most GRC-linked genes are species specific, a small conserved set predates the diversification of passerine birds 47 mya. Despite genic variability, GRCs are consistently repeat rich (63.7%-79.5%) and accumulate intact endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) with long terminal repeats (LTRs). This ERV proliferation peaked during the passerine radiation. In contrast, regular chromosomes purge ERVs to generate solo LTRs. Transcriptomic data reveal significantly higher ERV transcription on GRCs than on regular chromosomes in HF testis. We propose that GRCs act as reservoirs of active ERVs, potentially promoting germline transposition and accelerating speciation.

title: Infants respond to alterations in their own voice months before they recognize themselves in the mirror
abstract: Recognizing our body as our own grounds our perceptions, actions, and social interactions. Even newborns detect cross-modal links between self-related perceptions, 1 considered necessary for body ownership. 2 Yet, clear evidence for a sense of ownership only appears once children not simply detect but also correct mismatches between predicted and perceived self-related sensorimotor inputs. So far, this has mostly been measured using mirror self-recognition, which revealed that children typically do not start recognizing themselves before 18 months of age. 3 , 4 , 5 Infants rarely see their own face, however, and mirror self-recognition has been related to sensorimotor 6 and social experiences. 7 We therefore hypothesized that a sense of ownership over the voice might develop earlier, because most infants routinely perceive themselves vocalizing from birth. 8 , 9 , 10 This might allow them to build sensorimotor models supporting the identification of self-generated signals earlier in this modality. Related research with adults has used the altered auditory feedback paradigm to show that they respond to transpositions of the fundamental frequency (f 0 ) of their voice by restoring the alignment between predicted and perceived feedback. 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 Crucially, these compensatory changes depend on the voice being perceived as self-generated. 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 Using an adaptation of this paradigm with 5-month-old infants, we found that they can already perceive and correct upward transpositions of their f 0 , at an age when they remain unable to recognize themselves in the mirror. This suggests that hearing ourselves routinely allows us to learn what we sound like months before we recognize what we look like, which might be especially crucial for speech acquisition.

title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation
abstract: Knowing which way you are facing is essential for navigation. In animals, a dedicated set of neurons-head direction cells-acts as an internal compass: each cell fires most strongly when the animal faces a particular direction. The anterior thalamus is a key hub for this system. In humans, however, direct electrophysiological evidence for a comparable head direction signal remains limited. To address this gap, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) from the anteroventral thalamus (AVT) in patients with epilepsy while they performed a virtual navigation task. We analyzed neural activity during in-place rotation to isolate virtual head direction (vHD) information. Using inverted encoding models applied to multi-band neural activity, we reconstructed continuous vHD within two distinct virtual environments. Critically, the decoders failed to generalize across environments, indicating that the AVT vHD representation is environment specific rather than a fixed, universal map. This encoding was observed in the AVT and was temporally specific to rotation epochs; no significant encoding was detected in the pulvinar, another thalamic subregion not part of the classic head direction network in rodents. Together, these findings suggest that the human AVT carries environment-specific vHD information, bridging a gap between animal models and human navigation and highlighting a potential link to spatial disorientation disorders.

title: Effector-triggered immunity in oilseed crops is expanded despite the restricted specificity of the receptor ZAR1
abstract: Effector-triggered immunity (ETI), mediated by nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat immune receptors (NLRs), plays a critical role in protecting plants from pathogens. While the scope of ETI elicited by Pseudomonas syringae type III effectors on Arabidopsis thaliana has been characterized, no equivalent study has been performed on related oilseed crops, limiting our ability to translate fundamental plant immunity research into crop protection strategies. Here, we present a comprehensive screen of the ETI landscapes in Brassicaceous oilseeds Brassica napus (canola) and Camelina sativa (false flax) using 529 P. syringae effectors. We found that 44.6% and 55.4% of the 65 effector families contained alleles that elicited ETI in B. napus and C. sativa, respectively. Mapping ETI-elicitor homologs onto a P. syringae phylogeny revealed that 79% and 88% of strains carry three or more predicted ETI elicitors in B. napus and C. sativa, suggesting a significant ETI load against P. syringae in oilseeds. Oilseed ETI landscapes are expanded relative to A. thaliana, and the number of ETI responses is correlated with the species' NLR repertoire size and ploidy. Interestingly, while the A. thaliana ETI profile is smaller than the two oilseed crops, A. thaliana ETI responses are generally stronger. Further, the A. thaliana ZAR1 NLR has a broader effector recognition spectrum than ZAR1 in B. napus or C. sativa, supporting a role for convergent evolution in expanding immunodiversity. Overall, our findings reveal an expanded functional diversity of crop immune systems compared with a wild relative and highlight both ETI conservation and the divergence of recognition mechanisms.

title: Primary cilia mediate specific neuron-glia attachments in C. elegans through the secreted protein BUG-1
abstract: Primary cilia are signaling hubs that influence nearly every aspect of cell physiology. Neuronal primary cilia were recently found to form extensive attachments to glia in the mammalian brain, but it is not known how these attachments form or what functions they serve. Defects in cilia cause profound neurological disorders, highlighting the importance of understanding the specialized functions of neuronal cilia. Here, we use a genetic screen in Caenorhabditis elegans to determine how a stereotyped cilia-glia attachment forms and how the attachment affects ciliary calcium signaling. We find that two sensory neurons (URX and BAG) use their cilia to attach to a specific glial partner (ILsoL/R). This attachment requires BUG-1, a large secreted protein that localizes precisely to the cilia-glia attachment site. In the absence of BUG-1, neuronal cilia are present but always fail to attach to the glial cell. As a result, the URX cilia do not undergo activity-dependent remodeling seen in wild-type neurons and the BAG cilia exhibit reduced sensory stimulus-evoked calcium entry and defects in calcium clearance. Our work shows that cilia can select specific glial partners for attachment, identifies a novel protein that mediates these attachments, and demonstrates the functional consequences of loss of cilia-glia attachment on neuronal signaling. We propose that neuronal primary cilia act not only as antennae to receive long-range signals but also as points of close-range cell-cell contact, through which glia could modulate neuronal signaling.

title: A bacterial effector triggers dual-layer plant immunity through interaction with cell-surface and intracellular proteins
The rise and diversification of spidroins in the deep-time evolution of spiders
abstract: The evolutionary success of spiders is often attributed to their stunning ability to produce and utilize silk, but the potential link between the molecular and phenotypic basis of silk production and spider diversification is seldom tested in a robust dated phylogenetic framework. Here, we provide a macroevolutionary context for testing hypotheses by reconstructing and dating the spider tree of life using genomic and transcriptomic data. We searched exhaustively for members of the spider silk protein (spidroin) gene family from omics data and identified them in an iterative phylogenetic pipeline. Four distinct new types of spidroins with atypical sequence characteristics are discovered to be widespread in true spiders with the potential to affect silk properties, as inferred by our phylogenetic generalized linear mixed model and phylogenetic generalized least squares analyses. Combining our robust dated phylogenomic tree of spiders and a comprehensive spidroin dataset, a comprehensive picture of spidroin evolution is revealed. By performing state speciation and extinction analyses, we discovered that only the presence of aggregate gland is linked to a higher diversification rate among all binary spidroin-related characters, while the speciation rate of spiders is dependent on the number of ampullate-gland-associated-atypical spidroin types, silk gland types, total spidroin copies, and total spidroin types.

title: Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act
abstract: The US House's approval of the Sunshine Protection Act has revived the debate between permanent daylight saving time (DST) and standard time (ST). Permanent DST would push school start times before sunrise in many regions. Health, sleep, and scientific organizations favor permanent ST because it keeps solar, biological, and social time better aligned, 1 which matters most for children and adolescents, whose rigid school schedules already conflict with their biological night and are linked to poor sleep and reduced cognitive and academic performance. 2 , 3 , 4 The safety consequences of the proposed change remain unquantified, but for children, morning light availability matters most, since most return home in daylight regardless of clock policy. Using real school start times for 14 states that have approved permanent DST 5 and local sunrise times, we counted pre-sunrise commutes to school under each clock regime. Across the 14 states analyzed, permanent DST would require pre-sunrise departures for most of the winter, adding approximately 356 million days of pre-sunrise travel events among school-aged children (child days) relative to the current system (seasonally alternating between ST and DST). Applying the same approach nationwide, permanent DST would add more than 2 billion dark-morning commutes yearly. Analyzing a decade of national fatal crash records, we found higher odds of pedestrian involvement in dark-morning crashes than light-morning ones (odds ratio [OR] 1.77) and among pedestrians aged 5-18 (OR 2.22). Permanent DST would expose many more children to elevated pedestrian-crash risk, evidence that is relevant to the US' choice of a time standard.

title: Structural evolution of an ancient nucleotidyltransferase underlies divergence of AbiE antitoxins
abstract: Type VII toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems neutralize toxins through antitoxin-mediated post-translational modification (PTM), with the oligoAMPylation-based HepT/MntA and phosphorylation-based AbiE systems representing the most prevalent families. Although the AbiE TA system from Mycobacterium tuberculosis is known to employ antitoxin-dependent phosphorylation to antagonize its toxin, the overall distribution and regulatory diversity of AbiE-like systems remain obscure. A comprehensive search of the IMG/M database revealed that AbiE TA systems comprise a conserved toxin family paired with six distinct groups of antitoxins, including four newly identified antitoxin groups. Despite extensive sequence divergence, structural predictions indicate that most of these antitoxins share a conserved winged helix-turn-helix (wHTH) domain and a C-terminal structurally homologous domain (CTD). We further demonstrate a unifying antagonistic mechanism across these diverse systems: cognate antitoxins induce the phosphorylation of conserved serine or threonine residues in their partner toxins, resulting in toxin inactivation in a CTD-dependent manner. Structural analyses reveal that the antitoxin CTD exhibits homology to nucleotidyltransferases (NTases), including the AbiE toxin itself and the MntA antitoxins, suggesting that type VII antitoxins may have evolved from an ancestral NTase superfamily. Moreover, their DNA-binding capabilities are also diverse, with some functioning as transcriptional regulators and others lacking detectable DNA-binding activity. Collectively, this study expands the recognized diversity of type VII TA systems that rely on PTM for antagonism and provides new insights into their evolutionary trajectories.

title: Welwitschia leaf senescence is orchestrated via ERF113-ERF115-mediated antagonism between hormone signaling pathways
abstract: Phytohormone crosstalk is fundamental to plant development and adaptation. While the coordinated actions of different hormones are well recognized, the underlying molecular mechanisms in specific biological processes remain largely elusive. Here, we identified the WmERF113-WmERF115 module as a central hub that mediated jasmonic acid (JA)/abscisic acid (ABA)-gibberellins (GA) antagonism to regulate leaf senescence in Welwitschia, a desert plant with only two leaves that grow continuously over an exceptionally long lifespan. We revealed that the JA/ABA-inducible transcription factor (TF) WmERF113 directly activated senescence-associated genes (SAGs), promoting senescence and chlorophyll degradation, whereas the GA-responsive WmERF115 repressed the same targets to mitigate senescence. Notably, WmERF113 and WmERF115 physically interacted to form a heterodimer, mutually inhibiting each other's binding to target promoters. Furthermore, these two TFs acted as reciprocal trans-acting factors, repressing each other's expression through promoter cross-binding. This multiple-layer regulatory circuit ensured that leaf senescence of Welwitschia progressed in a temporally and spatially restricted manner. Our study provided an important conceptual framework in which phytohormone crosstalk was translated into TF antagonism for fine-tuning senescence, offering new insights into the adaptive strategies that enable plant survival in extreme environments.

title: Reduced dosage of phytochrome F engages SELF-PRUNING 6A to confer heat-resilient tuberization in potato
abstract: Natural variation at the earliness locus, or potato CDF1, enabled cultivated potato to overcome strict photoperiodic control of wild andigena landraces and tuberize under long days. Yet long-day conditions (LDs) are often associated with warm temperatures, which strongly suppress tuberization at night. With the rising ambient temperatures due to global warming, uncovering genetic factors that enable tuber formation under elevated temperatures has become a priority for breeding new cultivars with improved heat tolerance. Here we report that heat-resilient tuberization in potato can be unlocked by inactivating the photoreceptor phytochrome F (phyF) and optimized by exploiting its haploinsufficiency. Knockdown of phyF activates the SELF-PRUNING 6A (SP6A) tuberization-inducing signal and facilitates tuber formation under heat-stress conditions. Unexpectedly, loss of function of both SP6A and phyF still leads to early tuberization and heat escape, although it reduces the resilience of phyF mutants. Intriguingly, we show that haplotype-specific phyF editing in the 5' UTR or exonic regions leads to haploinsufficiency phenotypes enabling tuberization under heat-stress conditions, without other phytochrome-related penalties. Our results suggest that derepressing SP6A by a reduction of phyF dosage provides a key to unlock heat-resilient tuberization and highlight haploinsufficiency as a strategy for generating dominant alleles to enable rapid improvement of crops.

title: A putative structural transition underlies reliable formation of skeletal muscle
abstract: During organ development cells undergo significant morphological and positional changes. Yet, by the end of organogenesis, internal organ structure is typically robustly defined, with cells tightly packed. It remains an open question as to how the three-dimensional (3D) internal structure of an organ emerges reliably, particularly when there are multiple cell types interacting and dynamic boundary constraints. Here, we utilise quantitative live imaging and 3D morphological measures of the developing zebrafish myotome to unravel how early muscle organisation emerges. Contrary to the textbook view of muscle fibres as cylindrical, myocytes undergo an ordered chiral twist, the direction and magnitude of which depends on their position within the myotome. Further, cells skew and rearrange, seemingly to facilitate close packing of neighbouring muscle fibres. Cell movement undergoes a rapid decline in speed once the cells span the myotome segment. We find that cell packing is altered in mutants that disrupt cell fate or cell fusion, even though the final muscle segments remain largely confluent. Biophysical perturbation reveals that the cells are mechanically plastic, able to adjust to changes in the local cellular environment and boundary constraints. Taking these results together, we propose that the early myotome undergoes a structural transition, from a fluid-like state into a frozen state, resembling glass-like behaviour. Cellular plasticity in response to varying boundary constraints may be a general mechanism for ensuring robust organ morphogenesis in dense 3D tissues.

title: Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl
