title: Neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit regulates selective forgetting of olfactory learning
abstract: Forgetting is an active and essential process for adapting to constantly changing environments, yet the molecular and circuit mechanisms underlying selective forgetting remain poorly understood. Our previous studies in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans suggested that non-cell-autonomous neurosecretory signals accelerate forgetting of olfactory memory for diacetyl, an attractive odorant, by erasing its memory trace, which can be detected as changes in odor-evoked Ca 2+ responses in sensory neurons. However, the identity of the forgetting signal, the circuit through which it acts to erase the sensory memory trace, and the time window in which forgetting occurs have remained elusive. Here, we identify a neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic circuit in C. elegans that drives the selective forgetting of olfactory memory. Our genetic and imaging analyses revealed that the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-related neuropeptide NLP-47, secreted from AWC neurons, acts on its receptor GNRR-1 in AIZ interneurons. Glutamatergic neurotransmission from AIZ interneurons then erases the sensory memory trace in AWA neurons via GLR-4, an AMPA-type receptor expressed in AWA. Optogenetic silencing of AWC and AIZ showed that this circuit acts during the recovery phase following conditioning, defining a critical temporal window for active forgetting. This neuropeptidergic-glutamatergic pathway selectively promotes forgetting of a specific odorant memory without affecting another formed simultaneously. Together, our findings demonstrate that neuropeptidergic signaling promotes selective forgetting via a glutamatergic circuit, highlighting that active forgetting is regulated within a critical temporal window and with remarkable specificity.

title: Palaeobiology: The enzymes that made soft-tissue fossils scarce
abstract: Fossilised soft tissues offer exceptional glimpses of ancient biology. However, a new study of the evolution of decay enzymes suggests their proliferation over 500 million years ago contributed to the decline of soft tissue preservation, leaving the animal fossil record dominated by shells and skeletons.

title: Army ant raids connect terrestrial and aquatic food webs in mangroves
abstract: Army ant raids by Eciton burchellii parvispinum are iconic spectacles of Neotropical forests, driving ant-following birds and intense predation on leaf-litter arthropods 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . However, whether these terrestrial predators influence energy flows across ecosystem boundaries remains unknown. Apart from isolated natural history anecdotes, evidence for such interactions is lacking despite recognition that cross-ecosystem subsidies strongly affect food-web dynamics 5 , 6 , 7 . Here, we report a previously undescribed cross-ecosystem interaction in the mangroves of Yucatán, Mexico, where army ant raids trigger localized feeding aggregations among aquatic vertebrates. Stomach-content analyses of fishes attending raids at four independent Eciton colonies, complemented by observations across six colonies, show that prey escaping army ant predation can become a substantial terrestrial subsidy for resident fishes. This pulse was associated with marked shifts in fish diet and recurrent higher-order predator aggregations, revealing a pathway through which terrestrial predator effects can extend across ecosystem boundaries.

title: Heterodichogamy
abstract: Groh introduces the plant life history strategy heterodichogamy, or temporal separation of the sexes.

title: Hypothalamic cell-type differences associated with selection for tameness in the silver fox
abstract: The hypothalamus is a highly heterogeneous brain region that regulates fundamental physiological processes and behaviors, including innate social behaviors such as aggression, mating, and parenting 1 . Distinct cell types within hypothalamic nuclei have been linked to social behaviors, a principle established most clearly in mice, where manipulation of defined hypothalamic neuronal subtypes can initiate or suppress behaviors including attack, mounting, and parenting 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 . Whether hypothalamic cell types are modified as a result of selection during the evolution of social behavior remains unknown. Silver foxes (Vulpes vulpes) have been selectively bred for tame or aggressive behaviors and we have studied whether there are differences relating to these behaviors in the cellular makeup of the hypothalamus. We report here that tame foxes have fewer estrogen receptor-expressing neurons in the ventrolateral subdivision of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHvl) than aggressive foxes, and that this reduction is specific to a neuronal subtype linked to aggressive states in mice 5 . We have thus identified a candidate hypothalamic neuronal subtype associated with selection on social behavior during animal domestication.

title: Hippocampal–prefrontal cortical interactions and neural representations of memory
abstract: The ability to store memories and access past experiences when making decisions in the present is fundamental to cognition. The hippocampus is critical for these processes and has been a primary site of investigation in the learning and memory field for the last several decades. However, it is also clear that the hippocampus must work in concert with cortical brain regions to store and recall memories. Findings that demonstrate the necessity of hippocampal-medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) communication in these processes, as well as findings that link the mPFC to memory storage, retrieval, and decision-making, have contributed to this growing area of study. Here, we review our current understanding of three questions related to this communication. What information is represented in the hippocampus and the mPFC? What are the underlying neural activity patterns and brain states that facilitate communication of those representations? What impact do these patterns have on the ability to learn and remember in new and familiar settings? We highlight evidence for bidirectional communication both during and after experience, and we discuss areas of active investigation to further uncover the role of bidirectional hippocampal-cortical interactions in the formation and maintenance of neural representations of memory.

title: Deep-sea biology: Sisyphus on the bottom of the world
abstract: In Earth's most remote environments, at the bottom of the ocean, mineral-rich nodules litter the sea floor, attracting mining exploration. How do these nodules not get buried by sediment? New evidence suggests that small invertebrates living the fate of Sisyphus may provide an answer.

title: A socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey
abstract: Same-sex sexual behaviour is widespread in animals 1 , 2 , yet to our knowledge observations of such behaviour between individuals of different taxonomic families remain rare. In a grazing area on an Ethiopian plateau (Debre Libanos, Oromia), Achille, a bull (Bos taurus/indicus), and Patroclo, a male donkey (Equus asinus), actively engaged in reciprocal socio-sexual interactions, thus forming an unusual association. Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship. The interactions must have reproductive opportunity costs, in time and energy diverted away from potentially functional reproductive activities, and it would seem that these costs are outweighed by the strength of the animals' social bond 3 .

title: Fungal–bacterial interactions
abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.

title: Genome evolution: An archaeon stripped bare
abstract: A newly described archaeon has the smallest genome yet found in its domain, less than half the previous record, stripped of nearly all metabolism and retaining little beyond the machinery to replicate itself. Its biology and evolution remain enigmatic.

title: Plant domestication: Only a few generations connect three millennia of grapevine evolution
abstract: Genomic data from 28 archaeological grape pips trace the origins of Iberian grapevine cultivars from the Iron Age to the present. Grapevines introduced into Iberia from the east admixed with local wild populations, giving rise to Iberian cultivars, some of which are separated from modern varieties by only a handful of generations.

title: Biodiversity conservation: A fungus-free refuge for Colombia's amphibians
abstract: New research suggests that the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a high elevation biodiversity hotspot in northern Colombia, may be one of just a few places left on Earth where amphibian communities have not been affected by the fungal disease chytridiomycosis.

title: Neurofeedback: Training the brain from within
abstract: The hippocampus is a key brain structure linked to how we encode and reconstruct our own experiences. Neurofeedback training can help people identify strategies to successfully drive their own hippocampal activity, possibly promoting stronger encoding beyond the training session.

title: Sleep: And then there was light!
abstract: How has access to electricity impacted sleep in rural or urban environments? New research shows that electricity in previously unexposed communities delays and reduces sleep duration by about an hour in rural communities, but only delays sleep in urban communities.

title: Neuroscience: The architecture of a fear memory
abstract: Memories bind sensory, contextual, temporal, and affective features that support recall and flexible behavior. New research shows that the ventral region of the hippocampus represents these features in population activity, with similar temporal organization across learned and novel cues even as contributing neurons change.

title: Ajay Narendra
abstract: Ajay Narendra was born and raised in Bangalore, India, where he completed a bachelor's degree in Chemistry, Environmental Sciences and Zoology, with honours in Entomology from Bangalore University. He then earnt a master's degree in Remote Sensing and Cartography from Madurai Kamaraj University, before moving to Australia, where he wasawarded a PhD from Macquarie University and spent nine years as a postdoctoral fellow at the Australian National University. He then returned to Macquarie University, where he is currently a Professor of Invertebrate Neuroethology. His research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying spatial learning and memory, with a particular focus on how information is acquired, retained and translated into efficient navigation.

title: Conservation for cats of all sizes
abstract: Carnivore conservation gets the most attention when the biggest and most iconic species are involved, including lions, tigers, jaguars and cheetahs, but there is important work to be done to better understand the needs of smaller cats as well, including the Eurasian lynx, the Asian leopard cat and the South American tiger cat. Michael Gross reports.

title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration
abstract: Summary Microtubule dynamics regulation is critical for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, a.k.a. “tubulin autoregulation”, and TTC5 mutations are associated with cerebral atrophy, speech and motor impairment. Despite clinical relevance, the role of TTC5 and tubulin autoregulation in neurons has not been established. Using human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-derived cortical-like neurons, we demonstrate that tubulin autoregulation is active in neurons and fully TTC5-dependent. Loss of TTC5 function suppresses microtubule polymerization and impairs axonal outgrowth and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. These phenotypes recapitulate in vivo where TTC5 loss in mouse cerebral cortex projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and drives aberrant hypermigration. Patient disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking TTC5 dysfunction to clinically relevant neurological deficits. Together, our findings establish tubulin autoregulation and its mediators as essential regulators of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation
abstract: Abstract Neuronal function and survival depend on highly stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here we identified a role for SCAPER and TTC5, two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA autoregulation, in controlling neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scpr-1, ttc-5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that γ-tubulin nucleates MTs in the neuronal cell body from endosomal puncta, and that scpr-1 and ttc-5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to these structures. SCPR-1 is also instructive, as its overexpression drastically increases γ-tubulin levels and enhances MT density. We propose that these mechanisms are conserved since human SCAPER rescues C. elegans mutants, and SCAPER knockdown in rat hippocampal neurons reduces both γ-tubulin clustering at presynaptic sites and activity-dependent synaptic MT nucleation. Finally, while scpr-1, ttc-5, and γ-tubulin are not required for developmental axon elongation, they are essential for regeneration, where SCPR-1 directs γ-tubulin to the growth cone to facilitate regrowth following injury. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function, and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and microtubule nucleation.

title: Illusory cold desensitizes touch
Brain-wide activity imaging with electron microscopy reveals a distributed brain network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli
abstract: SUMMARY To understand how brains work, it is necessary to connect neural activity to synaptic-resolution circuit architecture. Recent advances in light-sheet microscopy (LSM) enable whole-brain, cellular-resolution imaging of activity of all neuronal cell bodies, however, most neurons from such datasets cannot be identified. In most organisms, neurons are identifiable based on their projections (and not based on their cell body position) which, when densely labelled, cannot be resolved using LSM. Here, we present a novel methodology to overcome this by combining whole-brain activity imaging with subsequent volume electron microscopy imaging of the same brain to visualise neuronal projections and identify neurons with interesting activity. We used this approach to identify brain neurons that process input from multisensory (nociceptive and mechanosensory) Basin interneurons that trigger vigorous escape in Drosophila larvae in response to threatening somatosensory stimuli. After whole-brain imaging of neuronal activity during Basin activation, we imaged the same brain with an enhanced focused ion-beam electron microscope (eFIB-SEM). We registered the functional and anatomical volumes and reconstructed (in the eFIB-SEM volume) the projections of neurons that responded to Basin activation to determine their developmental lineage and identity. This revealed a distributed network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli that trigger vigorous escape spanning 25 distinct lineages and many distinct brain areas, and included direct brain targets of Basin neurons that integrate somatosensory information with other modalities, as well as brain output neurons (descending neurons [DN]) that likely contribute to action-selection. Our workflow provides a powerful framework for mapping neuronal activity onto structure across an entire brain, yielding novel insights into the distributed central processing of noxious stimuli.

title: Hyperdivergent haplotypes control melanic camouflage in a polymorphic moth
abstract: Summary A majority of moths use melanic pigmentation to blend into the visual environment, and some species display genetically controlled color polymorphisms that provide tractable systems for dissecting the genetic basis of camouflage. Here we leveraged the natural polymorphism of Anticarsia gemmatalis moths to map a major-effect gene that controls melanic variation, and study its developmental roles using expression and loss-of-function assays. A genome-wide association mapping identifies the ivory:mir-193 non-coding RNA locus as a major locus of melanic variation, with highly-divergent haplotypes differentiating the Light and Dark morphs. Second, the expression of ivory:mir-193 prefigures the melanic coloration of each morph, and suggests that cis -regulatory variation at this locus determines the difference in adult pattern. Finally, CRISPR disruption of the ivory promoter and mir-193 hairpin region each abolish melanic scale pigmentation, demonstrating that this lnc-pri-miRNA module is required for dark-scale differentiation. These findings corroborate the emerging role of ivory:mir-193 as a key factor in the development of melanic patterning, and highlight its unique propensity to repeatedly drive phenotypic variation of adaptive potential in butterflies and moths. Highlights Anticarsia gemmatalis display striking variation in camouflage patterns Dark vs. Light color polymorphism map to the ivory:mir-193 hotspot locus Highly-diverged haplotypes drive morph-specific expression of ivory:mir-193 The miR-193 miRNA is required for melanic scale development Graphical Abstract

title: A female-specific RWP-RK transcription factor controls gamete differentiation and underlies anisogamy in the macroalga Bryopsis
